findings.issue_text: pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:37 — "entryPointAssetsCache   *dtos.EntryPointAssets // TODO: get rid of global state" The scalar process-global cache ignores cfg.StaticRootPath and the license-derived CDN even though both are function inputs, so after one non-dev server publishes assets every later server instance returns that first server's paths and the next multi-build or multi-tenant caller serves the wrong bundle; a single-server deployment merely masks this broken parameter contract. [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" Every concurrent non-dev cold-cache caller that observed nil queues on this lock and then sequentially rereads and republishes the manifest because the cache is never checked after lock acquisition, so startup latency grows linearly with the request burst; the RWMutex prevents a data race but does not coalesce initialization, which requires a second check or a once/singleflight-shaped cache. [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" Every development-mode call holds the process-global exclusive lock across the complete filesystem read and JSON decode despite development mode never returning the cached value, so concurrent index and recovery rendering form a global convoy and any new dev caller inherits that bottleneck; publication safety does not justify the lock because the dev branch can delete cache participation and load independently. [P3 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" Every concurrent non-development cold-cache caller that observed nil before blocking proceeds to reread the manifest after acquiring the lock because the cache is never rechecked inside the critical section, serializing duplicate initialization work instead of coalescing it [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" every concurrent non-development caller that observed the initial nil cache still reloads the manifest serially because the cache is not rechecked after acquiring the write lock, so a cold-start burst performs N ordered disk reads instead of one and the last redundant read can overwrite a valid cache entry with nil on failure [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" On every concurrent non-development cold-cache burst, callers that observed nil before waiting each acquire this lock and reload the manifest because the cache is never rechecked after locking, so the final artifact contradicts the stated frontend asset optimization by replacing one initialization with serialized repeated I/O; removing the data race does not preserve that intent because race-free coalesced initialization is simultaneously achievable [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" When concurrent non-development callers observe an empty cache, every waiter rereads the manifest after the first caller has populated it, so a transient failure in any redundant read returns an error and can replace a valid cache with nil for later callers; the RWMutex prevents a data race but does not defeat this missing post-lock cache check [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" The next concurrent development-mode asset reload serializes every developer request behind one process-wide lock held across the full filesystem read and JSON decode, so one slow or hung manifest read stalls all affected browser reloads indefinitely even after their contexts are canceled; cache-publication safety cannot justify this because development callers never consume the cache [P3 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:36 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu sync.RWMutex           // guard entryPointAssetsCache" This adds process-wide cache concurrency control that is not traceable to the sole stated requirement of frontend asset optimization and therefore constitutes unapproved scope drift [P2 confidence 100].

pkg/api/webassets/webassets.go:48 — "entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()" When concurrent callers observe an empty cache, every waiter takes this process-wide lock and redundantly rereads the manifest because the cache is never rechecked after locking, so a cold-start burst creates N serialized disk reads and exhausts waiting goroutines; the mutex's race prevention does not prevent this denial of service [P2 confidence 75].

goldens.comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the diff. After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check if entryPointAssetsCache is still nil before proceeding to reinitialize it. This means if multiple goroutines observe nil during the RLock phase and all block on Lock(), each one will sequentially re-read the manifest after acquiring the lock, even though the first one already populated the cache. This is a classic double-checked locking pattern that's missing the second check. The fix should re-check 'entryPointAssetsCache != nil' after acquiring the write lock to avoid redundant work.

The finding mischaracterizes a necessary concurrency fix as unauthorized scope expansion.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real issue in the diff. After acquiring the write lock at line 48, the code does not re-check if entryPointAssetsCache is still nil before proceeding to read the manifest. This means if multiple goroutines pass the initial RLock check when cache is nil, they will all queue up on the Lock(), and each one will redundantly re-read the manifest file even though the first one already populated the cache. This is a classic double-checked locking bug - the pattern requires re-checking the condition after acquiring the exclusive lock. While the severity of 'denial of service' may be slightly overstated, the redundant disk reads on cold start are a real correctness/performance issue introduced by this diff.
